claims.text: Mechanical-property variation among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets is primarily governed by lattice distortion.
The equiatomic quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has higher lattice distortion than its reduced-constituent subsets.
Severe lattice distortion produces wavy dislocation cores or dislocation lines that deviate from their glide planes.
Wavy dislocation cores resist dislocation motion.
Greater resistance to dislocation motion increases yield strength.
Greater resistance to dislocation motion lowers ductility.
Reducing the number of constituents reduces atomic-size mismatch and lattice distortion.
Lower lattice distortion permits easier dislocation glide.
Easier dislocation glide reduces yield strength.
Easier dislocation glide improves ductility.
The investigated initial materials are thermomechanically processed, single-phase FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and corresponding quaternary and ternary subsets.
Reduced-constituent variants will be made by selectively omitting one or more elements while retaining a single-phase FCC microstructure.
Identical thermomechanical processing will ensure comparable grain size and phase purity across compositions.
XRD peak broadening and lattice-parameter distributions can quantify lattice distortion in these alloys.
TEM can characterize local strain fields and dislocation-core structures relevant to the proposed mediator.
Quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower yield strength than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Quaternary and ternary alloys will have higher ductility than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
The predicted strength and ductility changes will occur together with measurable reductions in lattice-distortion indicators.
The hypothesis is limited to single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys processed under similar regimes and may fail when secondary phases or confounding microstructural features are present.
Grain size and residual stress may also affect the measured mechanical properties.
